item.title: ChatGPT gains native GIF creation with Images 2.6 update
item.description:
ChatGPT gains native GIF creation with Images 2.6 update

OpenAI has rolled out an update to ChatGPT that adds native animated GIF generation.

🔍 Overview

  • ChatGPT can now create GIFs from a text prompt or an uploaded photo.
  • The capability is part of the new Images 2.6 model.
  • Before this update, ChatGPT could not generate GIFs in a single step.

🧩 How it works

  • Users provide a prompt such as “can you make a gif of a cat dancing?” or upload an image.
  • The model returns an animated GIF and also offers controls to:
    • Adjust the animation speed.
    • Edit individual frames.
    • View the GIF frame by frame.
    • Share the result.

⚙️ Key details

  • Images 2.6 also speeds up regular image generation.
  • OpenAI reports that users now generate over 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT and its API, up from 3 billion in September.
  • New API variants introduced with the rollout:
Model Variant Capability
Images 2.6 Native GIF creation and faster image generation
GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare Faster image generation
GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst Higher‑quality image generation

🚀 Availability

  • Images 2.6 is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on web, desktop, and mobile apps.

💡 Why it matters

  • The update turns GIF creation into a native, single‑step operation within ChatGPT, expanding the range of media users can produce directly from text.

#OpenAI #ChatGPT #GIF #ImageGeneration

Source: ChatGPT will now make you animated GIFs

item.title: OpenAI introduces ChatGPT Images 2.5
item.description:
OpenAI introduces ChatGPT Images 2.5

OpenAI has released ChatGPT Images 2.5, an update to image generation models that have been used for more than 3 billion images across ChatGPT Images and the GPT‑Image models in the API.

⚙️ Key details

This latest release includes several improvements:

  • Faster response times
  • Better ability to preserve subjects in reference photos
  • Improved instruction-following ability across multiple turns

🚀 Availability

Two new model IDs are available in the API:

Model ID Use Case
gpt-image-2.5-sunburst Workflows where editing precision matters most
gpt-image-2.5-flare Fast, high-quality everyday image generation

#OpenAI #ChatGPT #ImageGeneration #API

Source: Introducing ChatGPT Images 2.5

item.title: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Images 2.5 and Sketch Feature
item.description:
OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Images 2.5 and Sketch Feature

OpenAI announced ChatGPT Images 2.5 on Tuesday, introducing updated image generation tools and a new feature called Sketch that allows users to use doodles as part of their prompts.

🧩 How it works

Users can now influence image generation through drawing and direct feedback:

  • Sketch: By typing @Sketch into the chat box, a window appears where users can draw a doodle and then tell ChatGPT how to make an image based on that sketch.
  • Direct Comments: Users can leave comments directly on specific parts of images to request changes, such as changing a cat’s eyes from blue to green.

⚙️ Key details

OpenAI stated that ChatGPT Images 2.5 provides several improvements over Images 2.0:

Feature Improvement
Visual Quality More natural lighting and richer textures
Instruction Following Better at following editing instructions across multiple turns
Performance Latency reduced by up to 50% compared with Images 2.0

🚀 Availability

ChatGPT Images 2.5 is currently available for the following users on desktop, mobile, and web:

  • ChatGPT users
  • ChatGPT Work users
  • Codex users

#OpenAI #ChatGPT #AIimages #ImageGeneration

Source: ChatGPT Sketch turns your bad drawings into detailed AI images

item.title: AI‑Generated Food Images Produce Uncanny, Incoherent Visuals
item.description:
AI‑Generated Food Images Produce Uncanny, Incoherent Visuals

🔍 Overview

“There is a torrent of unappetizing slop coming from restaurants, cafes, and brands that are increasingly turning to AI to generate images promoting their food.”

🧩 How Diffusion Models Work

“Put simply, diffusion models start with an image of pure noise — something like a screenful of static — and gradually remove noise little by little in order to create the requested visual.” “This means that initially coarse structures are recovered first with fine texture details” — Chris Russell, University of Oxford.

⚠️ Why the Images Look Wrong

  • The model can get the basic structure wrong early, then “lump vivid texture details on top of that structure.” (Russell)
  • “This is the same kind of failure as you see when a person is generated with six fingers instead of five.” (Russell)
  • “Diffusion models are notoriously weak at generating thin, continuous, terminating structures.” (Califano)
  • “Noodles, strands, and tendrils are exactly the kind of geometry that trips this up, so you get spaghetti‑like artifacts bleeding into places with no anatomical or culinary logic.” (Califano)
  • Repeating textures such as bubbles and seeds often spill into areas they should not be in. (Califano)
  • “AI image generation reproduces looks without proper knowledge about the world,” (Roland Meyer, University of Zurich).
  • “It doesn’t help that AI has no idea what a sandwich actually is. It has no understanding of the objects it’s creating or the physical world they inhabit.”
  • Food photography is highly stylized with sharp contrasts, intense colors, glossy lighting, and exaggerated shapes, which AI imitates without the professional aesthetic strategies behind them. (Meyer)
  • “These textures might look totally normal if used in an architectural context,” (Cook) “but they become wrong when we imagine it as edible food.”

🍴 Examples of AI‑Generated Food Failures

  • “donut shrimp”
  • “Reubens from the deep”
  • “wormlike noodles”
  • “noodle‑like pastries”
  • “stringy chicken”
  • “construction material masquerading as ice cream”
  • “ice cream masquerading as brains”
  • “monstrous attempt of a burger”
  • “trypophobic burrito from hell, grubs and all”

💡 Implications

  • The lack of world knowledge leads to objects that look plausible but defy culinary logic.
  • Training data and content associations are largely unknown, making it hard to predict or correct these failures. (Cook)
  • The mismatch between AI’s visual imitation and actual food aesthetics raises concerns for brands that rely on AI‑generated marketing imagery.

#AI #food #diffusionmodels #imagegeneration

Source: Why AI food looks like that
